The **governor-general of India** (1833 to 1950, from 1858 to 1947 the **Viceroy and Governor-General of India**, commonly shortened to **Viceroy of India**) was the representative of the monarch of the United Kingdom in their capacity as the emperor or empress of India and after Indian independence in 1947, the representative of the monarch of India. The office was created in 1773, with the title of governor-general of the Presidency of Fort William. The officer had direct control only over his presidency but supervised other East India Company officials in India. Complete authority over all of British territory in the Indian subcontinent was granted in 1833, and the official came to be known as the governor-general of India.
In 1858, because of the Indian Rebellion the previous year, the territories and assets of the East India Company came under the direct control of the British Crown; as a consequence, Company rule in India was succeeded by the British Raj. The governor-general headed the central government of India, which administered the provinces of British India, including Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Punjab, the United Provinces, and others.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_India#cite_note-3) However, much of India was not ruled directly by the British Raj; outside the provinces of British India, there were hundreds of nominally independent princely states or "native states", whose relationship was not with the British Indian government or the United Kingdom, but rather one of homage directly with the British monarch as sovereign successor to the Mughal emperors. From 1858, to reflect the governor-general's new additional role as the monarch's representative in response to the fealty relationships vis the princely states, the additional title of Viceroy was granted, such that the new office was entitled "Viceroy and Governor-General of India". This was usually shortened to "Viceroy of India" and was the head of government across much of Indian subcontinent.
The title of viceroy was abandoned when British India was partitioned into the two independent dominions of India and Pakistan, but the office of governor-general continued to exist in each country separately until they adopted republican constitutions in 1950 and 1956, respectively.

Until 1858, the governor-general was selected by the Court of Directors of the East India Company, to whom he was responsible. Thereafter, he was appointed by the sovereign on the advice of the British Government; the Secretary of State for India, a member of the British Cabinet, was responsible for instructing him on the exercise of their powers. After 1947, the sovereign continued to appoint the governor-general but thereafter did so on the advice of the government of the newly independent Dominion of India.
The governor-general served [at the pleasure of the sovereign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_His_Majesty's_pleasure "At His Majesty's pleasure"), though the practice was to have them serve five-year terms. A governor-general could have their commission rescinded; and if one was removed, or left, a provisional governor-general was sometimes appointed until a new holder of the office could be chosen. The first governor-general in India (of Bengal) was Warren Hastings, the first official governor-general of British India was Lord William Bentinck, and the first governor-general of the Dominion of India was Lord Mountbatten.
Warren Hastings, the first governor-general of Fort William from 1773 to 1785.
Lord William Bentinck, the first governor general of India from 1834 – 1835
Many parts of the Indian subcontinent were governed by the British East India Company (founded in 1600), which nominally acted as the agent of the Mughal emperor. Early British administrators were presidents or governors of the Bengal Presidency. In 1773, motivated by corruption in the Company, the British government assumed partial control over the governance of India with the passage of the Regulating Act 1773. A governor-general and Supreme Council of Bengal were appointed to rule over the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal. The first governor-general and Council were named in the Act.
The Charter Act 1833 replaced the governor-general and Council of Fort William with the governor-general and Council of India. The power to elect the governor-general was retained by the Court of Directors, but the choice became subject to the sovereign's approval via the India Board.

After the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the British East India Company's territories in India were put under the direct control of the sovereign. The Government of India Act 1858 vested the power to appoint the governor-general in the sovereign. The governor-general, in turn, had the power to appoint all lieutenant governors in India, subject to the sovereign's approval.
India and Pakistan acquired independence in 1947, but governors-general continued to be appointed over each nation until republican constitutions were written. Louis Mountbatten, 1st Earl Mountbatten of Burma, remained governor-general of India for ten months after independence, but the two nations were otherwise headed by native governors-general. India became a secular republic in 1950; Pakistan became an Islamic one in 1956.
Lord Curzon in his robes as viceroy of India, a post he held from 1899 to 1905.
Lord Mountbatten addressing the Chamber of Princes as Crown Representative in the 1940s
The governor-general originally had power only over the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal. The Regulating Act, however, granted the governor-general additional powers relating to foreign affairs and defence. The other presidencies of the East India Company (Madras, Bombay and Bencoolen) were not allowed to declare war on or make peace with an Indian prince without receiving the prior approval of the governor-general and Council of Fort William.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_India#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_India#cite_note-5)
The powers of the governor-general, in respect of foreign affairs, were increased by the [India Act 1784](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitt's_India_Act "Pitt's India Act"). The act provided that the other governors under the East India Company could not declare war, make peace or conclude a treaty with an Indian prince unless expressly directed to do so by the governor-general or by the Company's Court of Directors.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
The Regulating Act 1773 created the office with the title of Governor-General of the Presidency of Fort William, or **Governor-General of Bengal** to be appointed by the Court of Directors of the East India Company (EIC). The Court of Directors assigned a Council of Four (based in India) to assist the Governor-General, and the decision of the council was binding on the Governor-General from 1773 to 1784.
The Charter Act 1833 re-designated the office with the title of Governor-General of India. William Bentinck was the first to be designated as the Governor-general of India in 1833.
After the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the company rule in India was brought to an end, but the British India along with princely states came under the direct rule of the British Crown. The Government of India Act 1858 created the office of Secretary of State for India in 1858 to oversee the affairs of India, which was advised by a new Council of India with 15 members (based in London). The existing Council of Four was formally renamed as the Council of Governor-General of India or Executive Council of India. The Council of India was later abolished by Government of India Act 1935.

Following the adoption of the Government of India Act 1858, the Governor-General representing the Crown became known as the Viceroy. The designation 'Viceroy', although it was most frequently used in ordinary parlance, had no statutory authority, and was never employed by Parliament. Although the Proclamation of 1858 announcing the assumption of the government of India by the Crown referred to Lord Canning as "first Viceroy and Governor-General", none of the Warrants appointing his successors referred to them as 'Viceroys', and the title, which was frequently used in Warrants dealing with precedence and in public notifications, was one of ceremonies used in connection with the state and social functions of the Sovereign's representative. The Governor-General continued to be the sole representative of the Crown, and the Government of India continued to be vested in the appointments of Governor-General of India which were made by the British Crown upon the advice of **Secretary of State for India**. The office of Governor-General continued to exist as a ceremonial post in each of the new dominions of India and Pakistan, until they adopted republican constitutions in 1950 and 1956 respectively.

The **first Governor-General of Bengal** was **Warren Hastings** (1773–1785), appointed under the **Regulating Act, 1773**. The office gradually evolved — becoming **Governor-General of India** with the **Charter Act of 1833** (Lord William Bentinck being the first to hold that expanded title) and eventually becoming **Viceroy and Governor-General of India** after the **Government of India Act, 1858** when India came under direct Crown rule.
This is one of the most frequently tested topics in UPSC Prelims — the question often involves distinguishing between "first Governor-General of **Bengal**," "first Governor-General of **India**," and "first Viceroy of **India**."

## Understanding the Office
The title evolved through four phases:
| Period | Title | First Holder |  
| --- | --- | --- |  
| **1757-1774** | Governor of Bengal | Robert Clive |  
| **1774-1833** | **Governor-General of Bengal** | **Warren Hastings** |  
| **1833-1858** | **Governor-General of India** (under Company) | **Lord William Bentinck** |  
| **1858-1947** | **Viceroy and Governor-General of India** (under Crown) | **Lord Canning** |

## Understanding the Office
### Key Distinctions
*   **"First Governor-General of Bengal"** = Warren Hastings (1774)  
*   **"First Governor-General of India"** = Lord William Bentinck (1833) — through the Charter Act  
*   **"First Viceroy of India"** = Lord Canning (1858) — after the transfer of power to the Crown
All three are valid UPSC Prelims answers depending on the exact question wording.

## The Regulating Act of 1773
Before understanding Warren Hastings, we must understand the Act that created his position.

## The Regulating Act of 1773
### Background
By the 1770s, the East India Company faced several problems:
*   **Bankruptcy** — despite vast revenues from Bengal, the Company was nearly bankrupt  
*   **Corruption** — Company officials were personally enriching themselves (the "nabob" problem)  
*   **Political instability** — chaotic administration in Bengal after 1757  
*   **Bengal Famine (1770)** — killed ~10 million people while Company revenue continued extraction
The British Parliament decided to intervene — leading to the **Regulating Act of 1773**.

## The Regulating Act of 1773
### Key Provisions
| Provision | Significance |  
| --- | --- |  
| **Governor of Bengal** elevated to **Governor-General of Bengal** with oversight over Bombay and Madras presidencies | First move toward centralised British rule in India |  
| **Executive Council of 4 members** to assist the Governor-General | Checks on the Governor-General's power |  
| **Supreme Court of Judicature at Calcutta** established (1774) | First British court in India; jurisdiction over British subjects |  
| **End of Company's political role** — Company now answerable to British Parliament | British state control over Indian affairs |  
| Company employees forbidden from **private trade and gifts** | Attempted to reduce corruption |
The Regulating Act is often considered the **first major constitutional instrument for British India**.

## Warren Hastings: First Governor-General of Bengal (1774-1785)
### Background
**Warren Hastings** (1732-1818) had served the East India Company since 1750. By 1773, when he was appointed Governor-General of Bengal, he had over 20 years of Indian experience and knew Indian languages, culture, and politics well.

## Warren Hastings: First Governor-General of Bengal (1774-1785)
### Key Reforms and Actions
**Administrative:**
*   **Reduced corruption** among Company servants (at least to some degree)  
*   Established a more systematic **revenue administration**  
*   **Moved the Company's treasury** from Murshidabad to Calcutta (1772)  
*   Reorganised the judicial system
**Fiscal:**
*   **Abolished the Dual Government** system created by Robert Clive  
*   Brought Bengal's administration directly under Company control  
*   Introduced **settlement systems** for land revenue (though full reforms came under Cornwallis)
**Cultural and Intellectual:**
*   Founded the **Calcutta Madrasa (1781)** for Islamic studies  
*   Supported **William Jones's** founding of the **Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784)** — which initiated serious European scholarship on Indian languages and history  
*   Commissioned the first English translation of the **Bhagavad Gita** (1785)  
*   Supported the study of **Persian, Sanskrit, and Indian languages**

## Warren Hastings: First Governor-General of Bengal (1774-1785)
### Military Campaigns
Hastings's tenure saw several wars:
| War | Outcome |  
| --- | --- |  
| **First Anglo-Maratha War** (1775-82) | Ended in Treaty of Salbai (1782) — status quo ante |  
| **First Anglo-Mysore War** extended to his tenure (1780-84) | Ended in Treaty of Mangalore; Mysore not conquered |  
| **Rohilla War** (1774) | Awadh-British forces defeated Rohillas; controversial |

## Warren Hastings: First Governor-General of Bengal (1774-1785)
### The Impeachment Trial
After returning to England in 1785, Hastings was **impeached by the House of Commons** in **1787** on charges of:
*   Abuse of power  
*   Corruption  
*   Mismanagement  
*   Execution of Nanda Kumar  
*   Cruelty toward the Begums of Awadh  
*   Extortion from Chait Singh of Benares
The prosecution was led by **Edmund Burke**, one of the greatest orators of the time. The trial lasted from **1788 to 1795** — one of the longest trials in British history.
**Verdict:** Hastings was **acquitted of all charges**, but the proceedings severely damaged his reputation and finances. He died in 1818.
The impeachment trial is politically significant — it represented the first major British parliamentary scrutiny of colonial administration.

## Evolution to Governor-General of India
### Charter Act of 1833
The **Charter Act of 1833** made significant changes:
*   **Governor-General of Bengal** became **Governor-General of India**  
*   Governor-General now had authority over all British Indian territories  
*   The Madras and Bombay presidencies lost their power to make laws (only the Governor-General could legislate)
**Lord William Bentinck (1828-1835)** — already Governor-General of Bengal — became the **first Governor-General of India** when the Charter Act took effect in 1834.
Bentinck is famous for:
*   **Abolition of Sati** (1829)  
*   **English Education Act** (1835) — based on Macaulay's Minute  
*   Suppression of thuggee  
*   Introduction of **English** as the medium of instruction in higher education

## Transition to Viceroy (1858)
### Government of India Act, 1858
After the **1857 Revolt**, the **Government of India Act, 1858** transferred control of India from the East India Company to the British Crown. This created the title of **Viceroy**:
*   **Viceroy** represents the monarch (Queen/King of Britain)  
*   **Governor-General** is the administrative chief  
*   The same person held both titles simultaneously
**Lord Canning** (Governor-General since 1856) became the **first Viceroy** in 1858.
The title **"Viceroy and Governor-General of India"** continued until **1947**.

**Governor-General** of India was the **most senior administrative position** during **British India.** It was established through the **Regulating Act of 1773**, with **Warren Hastings serving as the 1st Governor-General of Bengal.** The **Charter Act of 1833** changed the nomenclature to **Governor-General of India**, and **Lord William Bentinck** served as the **1st person to be appointed to this position.** Following the **Government of India Act of 1858** after the Revolt of 1857, the Governor-General held the additional title of **Viceroy**, who served as a representative of the British monarch in India. **Lord Canning was the 1st Viceroy**.
The position underwent three major legal shifts, each reflecting a tighter grip by the British Parliament over Indian affairs:
| Phase | Title | Key Act | Purpose |  
| --- | --- | --- | --- |  
| **1773–1833** | **Governor-General of Bengal** | Regulating Act, 1773 | To control the corruption of EIC officials and centralize power in Calcutta. |  
| **1833–1858** | **Governor-General of India** | Charter Act, 1833 | To unify the administration of all British territories in India under one head. |  
| **1858–1947** | **Viceroy & Governor-General** | Govt. of India Act, 1858 | To represent the British Crown directly after the 1857 Revolt. |

*   Lord Mountbatten (1947) was the **last Viceroy of British India and the first Governor-General of independent India.**  
*   Lord Mountbatten executed the 3 June Plan that resulted in the Partition of British India and the emergence of India and Pakistan.  
*   Lord Mountbatten served as the first Governor-General of independent India from August 1947 to June 1948.

*   Lord Wavell (1944–1947) put forward the Wavell Plan and organized the Shimla Conference in 1945 to sort out the political disagreements among the Indian parties.  
*   The tenure of Lord Wavell also saw the Cabinet Mission of 1946 and the establishment of the Interim Government.

*   Lord Linlithgow (1936–1944) announced India to be a participant in World War II in 1939 without consulting any Indian political leader, resulting in the resignation of Congress Ministries.  
*   During his tenure, the Quit India Movement of 1942 took place followed by extensive arrest.

*   Lord Willingdon (1931–1936) was there for the Communal Award of 1932 and the Poona Pact between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B. R. Ambedkar thereafter.  
*   The Government of India Act, 1935, that provided for provincial autonomy and suggested the idea of All-India Federation was also enacted.

*   Lord Irwin (1926–1931) saw the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement and Dandi March in 1930.  
*   He made the Gandhi-Irwin Pact with Mahatma Gandhi in 1931 that enabled him to attend the Second Round Table Conference.

*   Lord Reading (1921–1926) saw the inception of the Swaraj Party in 1923 founded by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru.  
*   The Public Service Commission, the predecessor of present-day UPSC, was founded in 1926 as per the suggestions of Lee Commission.

*   Lord Chelmsford (1916–1921) was the period when Government of India Act, 1919, came into force.  
*   The Jallianwala Bagh Massacre took place during his tenure in 1919 and marked an important episode of India's freedom struggle.

*   Lord Hardinge II (1910–1916) saw the revocation of the Partition of Bengal in 1911.  
*   The British government declared the transfer of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi during the Delhi Durbar in the same year.

*   Lord Minto II (1905-1910) brought separate electorates for Muslims through the Indian Councils Act of 1909.  
*   S.P. Sinha became the first Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council during his term in office.

*   Lord Curzon (1899-1905) initiated the Partition of Bengal in 1905 that instigated the Swadeshi and boycott movement.  
*   He enacted the Indian Universities Act of 1904, thus increasing governmental interference in higher education.

*   Lord Elgin II (1894-1899) held office during the great famine in India in 1896-1897 that left its mark in the form of human misery and death.  
*   The tenure of Lord Elgin saw the killing of the British officers by the Chapekar brothers in 1897 due to the anti-plague policy imposed in Pune.

*   Lord Lansdowne (1888-1894) was the governor general during the implementation of Indian Councils Act of 1892.  
*   The Act provided expansion of legislative councils and indirect representation.  
*   The agreement made with Sir Mortimer Durand on the frontier between Afghanistan and British India in 1893 is also one of his accomplishments.

*   Lord Dufferin (1884-1888) was a witness to the formation of the Indian National Congress in 1885.

## The Regulating Act of 1773
### Background
By the 1770s, the East India Company faced several problems:
*   **Bankruptcy** — despite vast revenues from Bengal, the Company was nearly bankrupt  
*   **Corruption** — Company officials were personally enriching themselves (the "nabob" problem)  
*   **Political instability** — chaotic administration in Bengal after 1757  
*   **Bengal Famine (1770)** — killed ~10 million people while Company revenue continued extraction
The British Parliament decided to intervene — leading to the **Regulating Act of 1773**.

## The Regulating Act of 1773
### Key Provisions
| Provision | Significance |  
| --- | --- |  
| **Governor of Bengal** elevated to **Governor-General of Bengal** with oversight over Bombay and Madras presidencies | First move toward centralised British rule in India |  
| **Executive Council of 4 members** to assist the Governor-General | Checks on the Governor-General's power |  
| **Supreme Court of Judicature at Calcutta** established (1774) | First British court in India; jurisdiction over British subjects |  
| **End of Company's political role** — Company now answerable to British Parliament | British state control over Indian affairs |  
| Company employees forbidden from **private trade and gifts** | Attempted to reduce corruption |
The Regulating Act is often considered the **first major constitutional instrument for British India**.

## Warren Hastings: First Governor-General of Bengal (1774-1785)
### Background
**Warren Hastings** (1732-1818) had served the East India Company since 1750. By 1773, when he was appointed Governor-General of Bengal, he had over 20 years of Indian experience and knew Indian languages, culture, and politics well.

## Warren Hastings: First Governor-General of Bengal (1774-1785)
### Key Reforms and Actions
**Administrative:**
*   **Reduced corruption** among Company servants (at least to some degree)  
*   Established a more systematic **revenue administration**  
*   **Moved the Company's treasury** from Murshidabad to Calcutta (1772)  
*   Reorganised the judicial system
**Fiscal:**
*   **Abolished the Dual Government** system created by Robert Clive  
*   Brought Bengal's administration directly under Company control  
*   Introduced **settlement systems** for land revenue (though full reforms came under Cornwallis)
**Cultural and Intellectual:**
*   Founded the **Calcutta Madrasa (1781)** for Islamic studies  
*   Supported **William Jones's** founding of the **Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784)** — which initiated serious European scholarship on Indian languages and history  
*   Commissioned the first English translation of the **Bhagavad Gita** (1785)  
*   Supported the study of **Persian, Sanskrit, and Indian languages**

## Warren Hastings: First Governor-General of Bengal (1774-1785)
### The Impeachment Trial
After returning to England in 1785, Hastings was **impeached by the House of Commons** in **1787** on charges of:
*   Abuse of power  
*   Corruption  
*   Mismanagement  
*   Execution of Nanda Kumar  
*   Cruelty toward the Begums of Awadh  
*   Extortion from Chait Singh of Benares
The prosecution was led by **Edmund Burke**, one of the greatest orators of the time. The trial lasted from **1788 to 1795** — one of the longest trials in British history.
**Verdict:** Hastings was **acquitted of all charges**, but the proceedings severely damaged his reputation and finances. He died in 1818.
The impeachment trial is politically significant — it represented the first major British parliamentary scrutiny of colonial administration.

## Evolution to Governor-General of India
### Charter Act of 1833
The **Charter Act of 1833** made significant changes:
*   **Governor-General of Bengal** became **Governor-General of India**  
*   Governor-General now had authority over all British Indian territories  
*   The Madras and Bombay presidencies lost their power to make laws (only the Governor-General could legislate)
**Lord William Bentinck (1828-1835)** — already Governor-General of Bengal — became the **first Governor-General of India** when the Charter Act took effect in 1834.
Bentinck is famous for:
*   **Abolition of Sati** (1829)  
*   **English Education Act** (1835) — based on Macaulay's Minute  
*   Suppression of thuggee  
*   Introduction of **English** as the medium of instruction in higher education

## Transition to Viceroy (1858)
### Government of India Act, 1858
After the **1857 Revolt**, the **Government of India Act, 1858** transferred control of India from the East India Company to the British Crown. This created the title of **Viceroy**:
*   **Viceroy** represents the monarch (Queen/King of Britain)  
*   **Governor-General** is the administrative chief  
*   The same person held both titles simultaneously
**Lord Canning** (Governor-General since 1856) became the **first Viceroy** in 1858.
The title **"Viceroy and Governor-General of India"** continued until **1947**.

The **governor-general of India** (1833 to 1950, from 1858 to 1947 the **Viceroy and Governor-General of India**, commonly shortened to **Viceroy of India**) was the representative of the monarch of the United Kingdom in their capacity as the emperor or empress of India and after Indian independence in 1947, the representative of the monarch of India. The office was created in 1773, with the title of governor-general of the Presidency of Fort William. The officer had direct control only over his presidency but supervised other East India Company officials in India. Complete authority over all of British territory in the Indian subcontinent was granted in 1833, and the official came to be known as the governor-general of India.
In 1858, because of the Indian Rebellion the previous year, the territories and assets of the East India Company came under the direct control of the British Crown; as a consequence, Company rule in India was succeeded by the British Raj. The governor-general headed the central government of India, which administered the provinces of British India, including Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Punjab, the United Provinces, and others.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_India#cite_note-3) However, much of India was not ruled directly by the British Raj; outside the provinces of British India, there were hundreds of nominally independent princely states or "native states", whose relationship was not with the British Indian government or the United Kingdom, but rather one of homage directly with the British monarch as sovereign successor to the Mughal emperors. From 1858, to reflect the governor-general's new additional role as the monarch's representative in response to the fealty relationships vis the princely states, the additional title of Viceroy was granted, such that the new office was entitled "Viceroy and Governor-General of India". This was usually shortened to "Viceroy of India" and was the head of government across much of Indian subcontinent.
The title of viceroy was abandoned when British India was partitioned into the two independent dominions of India and Pakistan, but the office of governor-general continued to exist in each country separately until they adopted republican constitutions in 1950 and 1956, respectively.

Until 1858, the governor-general was selected by the Court of Directors of the East India Company, to whom he was responsible. Thereafter, he was appointed by the sovereign on the advice of the British Government; the Secretary of State for India, a member of the British Cabinet, was responsible for instructing him on the exercise of their powers. After 1947, the sovereign continued to appoint the governor-general but thereafter did so on the advice of the government of the newly independent Dominion of India.
The governor-general served [at the pleasure of the sovereign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_His_Majesty's_pleasure "At His Majesty's pleasure"), though the practice was to have them serve five-year terms. A governor-general could have their commission rescinded; and if one was removed, or left, a provisional governor-general was sometimes appointed until a new holder of the office could be chosen. The first governor-general in India (of Bengal) was Warren Hastings, the first official governor-general of British India was Lord William Bentinck, and the first governor-general of the Dominion of India was Lord Mountbatten.
Warren Hastings, the first governor-general of Fort William from 1773 to 1785.

Many parts of the Indian subcontinent were governed by the British East India Company (founded in 1600), which nominally acted as the agent of the Mughal emperor. Early British administrators were presidents or governors of the Bengal Presidency. In 1773, motivated by corruption in the Company, the British government assumed partial control over the governance of India with the passage of the Regulating Act 1773. A governor-general and Supreme Council of Bengal were appointed to rule over the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal. The first governor-general and Council were named in the Act.
The Charter Act 1833 replaced the governor-general and Council of Fort William with the governor-general and Council of India. The power to elect the governor-general was retained by the Court of Directors, but the choice became subject to the sovereign's approval via the India Board.

After the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the British East India Company's territories in India were put under the direct control of the sovereign. The Government of India Act 1858 vested the power to appoint the governor-general in the sovereign. The governor-general, in turn, had the power to appoint all lieutenant governors in India, subject to the sovereign's approval.
India and Pakistan acquired independence in 1947, but governors-general continued to be appointed over each nation until republican constitutions were written. Louis Mountbatten, 1st Earl Mountbatten of Burma, remained governor-general of India for ten months after independence, but the two nations were otherwise headed by native governors-general. India became a secular republic in 1950; Pakistan became an Islamic one in 1956.

The governor-general originally had power only over the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal. The Regulating Act, however, granted the governor-general additional powers relating to foreign affairs and defence. The other presidencies of the East India Company (Madras, Bombay and Bencoolen) were not allowed to declare war on or make peace with an Indian prince without receiving the prior approval of the governor-general and Council of Fort William.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_India#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_India#cite_note-5)
The powers of the governor-general, in respect of foreign affairs, were increased by the [India Act 1784](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitt's_India_Act "Pitt's India Act"). The act provided that the other governors under the East India Company could not declare war, make peace or conclude a treaty with an Indian prince unless expressly directed to do so by the governor-general or by the Company's Court of Directors.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
The Regulating Act 1773 created the office with the title of Governor-General of the Presidency of Fort William, or **Governor-General of Bengal** to be appointed by the Court of Directors of the East India Company (EIC). The Court of Directors assigned a Council of Four (based in India) to assist the Governor-General, and the decision of the council was binding on the Governor-General from 1773 to 1784.
The Charter Act 1833 re-designated the office with the title of Governor-General of India. William Bentinck was the first to be designated as the Governor-general of India in 1833.
After the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the company rule in India was brought to an end, but the British India along with princely states came under the direct rule of the British Crown. The Government of India Act 1858 created the office of Secretary of State for India in 1858 to oversee the affairs of India, which was advised by a new Council of India with 15 members (based in London). The existing Council of Four was formally renamed as the Council of Governor-General of India or Executive Council of India. The Council of India was later abolished by Government of India Act 1935.
texts.1: Following the adoption of the Government of India Act 1858, the Governor-General representing the Crown became known as the Viceroy. The designation 'Viceroy', although it was most frequently used in ordinary parlance, had no statutory authority, and was never employed by Parliament. Although the Proclamation of 1858 announcing the assumption of the government of India by the Crown referred to Lord Canning as "first Viceroy and Governor-General", none of the Warrants appointing his successors referred to them as 'Viceroys', and the title, which was frequently used in Warrants dealing with precedence and in public notifications, was one of ceremonies used in connection with the state and social functions of the Sovereign's representative. The Governor-General continued to be the sole representative of the Crown, and the Government of India continued to be vested in the appointments of Governor-General of India which were made by the British Crown upon the advice of **Secretary of State for India**. The office of Governor-General continued to exist as a ceremonial post in each of the new dominions of India and Pakistan, until they adopted republican constitutions in 1950 and 1956 respectively.

The office gradually evolved — becoming **Governor-General of India** with the **Charter Act of 1833** (Lord William Bentinck being the first to hold that expanded title) and eventually becoming **Viceroy and Governor-General of India** after the **Government of India Act, 1858** when India came under direct Crown rule.
This is one of the most frequently tested topics in UPSC Prelims — the question often involves distinguishing between "first Governor-General of **Bengal**," "first Governor-General of **India**," and "first Viceroy of **India**."

## Understanding the Office
The title evolved through four phases:
| Period | Title | First Holder |  
| --- | --- | --- |  
| **1757-1774** | Governor of Bengal | Robert Clive |  
| **1774-1833** | **Governor-General of Bengal** | **Warren Hastings** |  
| **1833-1858** | **Governor-General of India** (under Company) | **Lord William Bentinck** |  
| **1858-1947** | **Viceroy and Governor-General of India** (under Crown) | **Lord Canning** |

## Understanding the Office
### Key Distinctions
*   **"First Governor-General of Bengal"** = Warren Hastings (1774)  
*   **"First Governor-General of India"** = Lord William Bentinck (1833) — through the Charter Act  
*   **"First Viceroy of India"** = Lord Canning (1858) — after the transfer of power to the Crown
All three are valid UPSC Prelims answers depending on the exact question wording.

## The Regulating Act of 1773
Before understanding Warren Hastings, we must understand the Act that created his position.

## The Regulating Act of 1773
### Background
By the 1770s, the East India Company faced several problems:
*   **Bankruptcy** — despite vast revenues from Bengal, the Company was nearly bankrupt  
*   **Corruption** — Company officials were personally enriching themselves (the "nabob" problem)  
*   **Political instability** — chaotic administration in Bengal after 1757  
*   **Bengal Famine (1770)** — killed ~10 million people while Company revenue continued extraction
The British Parliament decided to intervene — leading to the **Regulating Act of 1773**.

## The Regulating Act of 1773
### Key Provisions
| Provision | Significance |  
| --- | --- |  
| **Governor of Bengal** elevated to **Governor-General of Bengal** with oversight over Bombay and Madras presidencies | First move toward centralised British rule in India |  
| **Executive Council of 4 members** to assist the Governor-General | Checks on the Governor-General's power |  
| **Supreme Court of Judicature at Calcutta** established (1774) | First British court in India; jurisdiction over British subjects |  
| **End of Company's political role** — Company now answerable to British Parliament | British state control over Indian affairs |  
| Company employees forbidden from **private trade and gifts** | Attempted to reduce corruption |
The Regulating Act is often considered the **first major constitutional instrument for British India**.

## Warren Hastings: First Governor-General of Bengal (1774-1785)
### Background
**Warren Hastings** (1732-1818) had served the East India Company since 1750. By 1773, when he was appointed Governor-General of Bengal, he had over 20 years of Indian experience and knew Indian languages, culture, and politics well.

## Warren Hastings: First Governor-General of Bengal (1774-1785)
### Key Reforms and Actions
**Administrative:**
*   **Reduced corruption** among Company servants (at least to some degree)  
*   Established a more systematic **revenue administration**  
*   **Moved the Company's treasury** from Murshidabad to Calcutta (1772)  
*   Reorganised the judicial system
**Fiscal:**
*   **Abolished the Dual Government** system created by Robert Clive  
*   Brought Bengal's administration directly under Company control  
*   Introduced **settlement systems** for land revenue (though full reforms came under Cornwallis)
**Cultural and Intellectual:**
*   Founded the **Calcutta Madrasa (1781)** for Islamic studies  
*   Supported **William Jones's** founding of the **Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784)** — which initiated serious European scholarship on Indian languages and history  
*   Commissioned the first English translation of the **Bhagavad Gita** (1785)  
*   Supported the study of **Persian, Sanskrit, and Indian languages**

## Warren Hastings: First Governor-General of Bengal (1774-1785)
### Military Campaigns
Hastings's tenure saw several wars:
| War | Outcome |  
| --- | --- |  
| **First Anglo-Maratha War** (1775-82) | Ended in Treaty of Salbai (1782) — status quo ante |  
| **First Anglo-Mysore War** extended to his tenure (1780-84) | Ended in Treaty of Mangalore; Mysore not conquered |  
| **Rohilla War** (1774) | Awadh-British forces defeated Rohillas; controversial |

## Warren Hastings: First Governor-General of Bengal (1774-1785)
### The Impeachment Trial
After returning to England in 1785, Hastings was **impeached by the House of Commons** in **1787** on charges of:
*   Abuse of power  
*   Corruption  
*   Mismanagement  
*   Execution of Nanda Kumar  
*   Cruelty toward the Begums of Awadh  
*   Extortion from Chait Singh of Benares
The prosecution was led by **Edmund Burke**, one of the greatest orators of the time. The trial lasted from **1788 to 1795** — one of the longest trials in British history.
**Verdict:** Hastings was **acquitted of all charges**, but the proceedings severely damaged his reputation and finances. He died in 1818.
The impeachment trial is politically significant — it represented the first major British parliamentary scrutiny of colonial administration.

## Evolution to Governor-General of India
### Charter Act of 1833
The **Charter Act of 1833** made significant changes:
*   **Governor-General of Bengal** became **Governor-General of India**  
*   Governor-General now had authority over all British Indian territories  
*   The Madras and Bombay presidencies lost their power to make laws (only the Governor-General could legislate)
**Lord William Bentinck (1828-1835)** — already Governor-General of Bengal — became the **first Governor-General of India** when the Charter Act took effect in 1834.
Bentinck is famous for:
*   **Abolition of Sati** (1829)  
*   **English Education Act** (1835) — based on Macaulay's Minute  
*   Suppression of thuggee  
*   Introduction of **English** as the medium of instruction in higher education

## Transition to Viceroy (1858)
### Government of India Act, 1858
After the **1857 Revolt**, the **Government of India Act, 1858** transferred control of India from the East India Company to the British Crown. This created the title of **Viceroy**:
*   **Viceroy** represents the monarch (Queen/King of Britain)  
*   **Governor-General** is the administrative chief  
*   The same person held both titles simultaneously
**Lord Canning** (Governor-General since 1856) became the **first Viceroy** in 1858.
The title **"Viceroy and Governor-General of India"** continued until **1947**.

The **governor-general of India** (1833 to 1950, from 1858 to 1947 the **Viceroy and Governor-General of India**, commonly shortened to **Viceroy of India**) was the representative of the monarch of the United Kingdom in their capacity as the emperor or empress of India and after Indian independence in 1947, the representative of the monarch of India. The office was created in 1773, with the title of governor-general of the Presidency of Fort William. The officer had direct control only over his presidency but supervised other East India Company officials in India. Complete authority over all of British territory in the Indian subcontinent was granted in 1833, and the official came to be known as the governor-general of India.
In 1858, because of the Indian Rebellion the previous year, the territories and assets of the East India Company came under the direct control of the British Crown; as a consequence, Company rule in India was succeeded by the British Raj. The governor-general headed the central government of India, which administered the provinces of British India, including Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Punjab, the United Provinces, and others.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_India#cite_note-3) However, much of India was not ruled directly by the British Raj; outside the provinces of British India, there were hundreds of nominally independent princely states or "native states", whose relationship was not with the British Indian government or the United Kingdom, but rather one of homage directly with the British monarch as sovereign successor to the Mughal emperors. From 1858, to reflect the governor-general's new additional role as the monarch's representative in response to the fealty relationships vis the princely states, the additional title of Viceroy was granted, such that the new office was entitled "Viceroy and Governor-General of India". This was usually shortened to "Viceroy of India" and was the head of government across much of Indian subcontinent.
The title of viceroy was abandoned when British India was partitioned into the two independent dominions of India and Pakistan, but the office of governor-general continued to exist in each country separately until they adopted republican constitutions in 1950 and 1956, respectively.

Until 1858, the governor-general was selected by the Court of Directors of the East India Company, to whom he was responsible. Thereafter, he was appointed by the sovereign on the advice of the British Government; the Secretary of State for India, a member of the British Cabinet, was responsible for instructing him on the exercise of their powers. After 1947, the sovereign continued to appoint the governor-general but thereafter did so on the advice of the government of the newly independent Dominion of India.
The governor-general served [at the pleasure of the sovereign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_His_Majesty's_pleasure "At His Majesty's pleasure"), though the practice was to have them serve five-year terms. A governor-general could have their commission rescinded; and if one was removed, or left, a provisional governor-general was sometimes appointed until a new holder of the office could be chosen. The first governor-general in India (of Bengal) was Warren Hastings, the first official governor-general of British India was Lord William Bentinck, and the first governor-general of the Dominion of India was Lord Mountbatten.

Early British administrators were presidents or governors of the Bengal Presidency. In 1773, motivated by corruption in the Company, the British government assumed partial control over the governance of India with the passage of the Regulating Act 1773. A governor-general and Supreme Council of Bengal were appointed to rule over the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal. The first governor-general and Council were named in the Act.
The Charter Act 1833 replaced the governor-general and Council of Fort William with the governor-general and Council of India. The power to elect the governor-general was retained by the Court of Directors, but the choice became subject to the sovereign's approval via the India Board.

After the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the British East India Company's territories in India were put under the direct control of the sovereign. The Government of India Act 1858 vested the power to appoint the governor-general in the sovereign. The governor-general, in turn, had the power to appoint all lieutenant governors in India, subject to the sovereign's approval.
India and Pakistan acquired independence in 1947, but governors-general continued to be appointed over each nation until republican constitutions were written. Louis Mountbatten, 1st Earl Mountbatten of Burma, remained governor-general of India for ten months after independence, but the two nations were otherwise headed by native governors-general. India became a secular republic in 1950; Pakistan became an Islamic one in 1956.

The Regulating Act 1773 created the office with the title of Governor-General of the Presidency of Fort William, or **Governor-General of Bengal** to be appointed by the Court of Directors of the East India Company (EIC). The Court of Directors assigned a Council of Four (based in India) to assist the Governor-General, and the decision of the council was binding on the Governor-General from 1773 to 1784.
The Charter Act 1833 re-designated the office with the title of Governor-General of India. William Bentinck was the first to be designated as the Governor-general of India in 1833.
After the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the company rule in India was brought to an end, but the British India along with princely states came under the direct rule of the British Crown. The Government of India Act 1858 created the office of Secretary of State for India in 1858 to oversee the affairs of India, which was advised by a new Council of India with 15 members (based in London). The existing Council of Four was formally renamed as the Council of Governor-General of India or Executive Council of India. The Council of India was later abolished by Government of India Act 1935.

Following the adoption of the Government of India Act 1858, the Governor-General representing the Crown became known as the Viceroy. The designation 'Viceroy', although it was most frequently used in ordinary parlance, had no statutory authority, and was never employed by Parliament. Although the Proclamation of 1858 announcing the assumption of the government of India by the Crown referred to Lord Canning as "first Viceroy and Governor-General", none of the Warrants appointing his successors referred to them as 'Viceroys', and the title, which was frequently used in Warrants dealing with precedence and in public notifications, was one of ceremonies used in connection with the state and social functions of the Sovereign's representative. The Governor-General continued to be the sole representative of the Crown, and the Government of India continued to be vested in the appointments of Governor-General of India which were made by the British Crown upon the advice of **Secretary of State for India**. The office of Governor-General continued to exist as a ceremonial post in each of the new dominions of India and Pakistan, until they adopted republican constitutions in 1950 and 1956 respectively.

- **Significance**: When the Charter Act of 1833 re-designated the office from "Governor-General of Bengal" to "Governor-General of India," he became the first to hold this specific title
- This is typically the answer expected when asking specifically about "first Governor-General of **India**"

### **Warren Hastings** (1773–1785)
- **Title**: First **Governor-General of Bengal** (Governor-General of the Presidency of Fort William)
- **Significance**: He was the first person to hold any governor-generalship position in India, but his official title was "Governor-General of Bengal" until 1833
- Under the Regulating Act of 1773, this was the highest position available in India at the time
